Math 237, Project 1: Finding Diamond in the Rough Songs in Spotify¶

Research Question¶

  • What characteristics do popular songs have?
  • From those characteristics, what are some songs that have those characteristics that are not popular?
    • Would this song make us social media famous? (We assume the song would make us famous, because typically if a song is popular on spotify, it would be popular on social media)

Spotify Dataset¶

  • A dataset of Spotify songs with different genres and their audio features
  • The way the data was obtained is unknown, but it is assumed that it was retrieved by data scraping

Data Dictionary¶

Source: Maharshi Pandya (2022), Spotify Tracks Dataset. https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/maharshipandya/-spotify-tracks-dataset/data

Column Type Meaning
track_id categorical The Spotify ID for the track
artists categorical The artists' names who performed the track. If there is more than one artist, they are separated by a ;
album_name categorical The album name in which the track appears
track_name categorical Name of the track
explicit categorical Whether or not the track has explicit lyrics (true = yes it does; false = no it does not OR unknown)
track_genre categorical The genre in which the track belongs
popularity numerical The popularity of a track is a value between 0 and 100, with 100 being the most popular
duration_ms numerical The track length in milliseconds
danceability numerical Danceability describes how suitable a track is for dancing based on a combination of musical elements including tempo, rhythm stability, beat strength, and overall regularity. A value of 0.0 is least danceable and 1.0 is most danceable
energy numerical Energy is a measure from 0.0 to 1.0 and represents a perceptual measure of intensity and activity. Typically, energetic tracks feel fast, loud, and noisy. For example, death metal has high energy, while a Bach prelude scores low on the scale
key numerical The key the track is in. Integers map to pitches using standard Pitch Class notation. E.g. 0 = C, 1 = C♯/D♭, 2 = D, and so on. If no key was detected, the value is -1
loudness numerical The overall loudness of a track in decibels (dB)
mode numerical Mode indicates the modality (major or minor) of a track, the type of scale from which its melodic content is derived. Major is represented by 1 and minor is 0

| speechiness | numerical | Speechiness detects the presence of spoken words in a track. The more exclusively speech-like the recording (e.g. talk show, audio book, poetry), the closer to 1.0 the attribute value. Values above 0.66 describe tracks that are probably made ||| entirely of spoken words. Values between 0.33 and 0.66 describe tracks that may contain both music and speech, either in sections or layered, including such cases as rap music. Values below 0.33 most likely represent music and other non-speech-like tracks | | acousticness | numerical | A confidence measure from 0.0 to 1.0 of whether the track is acoustic. 1.0 represents high confidence the track is acoustic | | instrumentalness | numerical | Predicts whether a track contains no vocals. "Ooh" and "aah" sounds are treated as instrumental in this context. Rap or spoken word tracks are clearly "vocal". The closer the instrumentalness value is to 1.0, the greater likelihood the track contains no vocal content | | liveness | numerical | Detects the presence of an audience in the recording. Higher liveness values represent an increased probability that the track was performed live. A value above 0.8 provides strong likelihood that the track is live | | valence | numerical | A measure from 0.0 to 1.0 describing the musical positiveness conveyed by a track. Tracks with high valence sound more positive (e.g. happy, cheerful, euphoric), while tracks with low valence sound more negative (e.g. sad, depressed, angry) | | tempo | numerical |The overall estimated tempo of a track in beats per minute (BPM). In musical terminology, tempo is the speed or pace of a given piece and derives directly from the average beat duration | | time_signature | numerical | An estimated time signature. The time signature (meter) is a notational convention to specify how many beats are in each bar (or measure). The time signature ranges from 3 to 7 indicating time signatures of 3/4, to 7/4. |

Now that our data has been cleaned up, we will compare different variables to popularity to find traits that popular songs have.

Before findinging traits of popular songs, we decided to understand how the popularity of songs are distributed.

# Histogram of Popularity
plt.hist(dataV2['popularity'], bins =20)
plt.xlabel('Popularity', fontsize = 16)
plt.ylabel('Number of Cases', fontsize = 16)
plt.title('Histogram of Popularity', fontsize = 18)

Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Histogram of Popularity')

There is unusually, a high bar at the 'popularity' == 0 bar, so we decided to see how many there are.

#Code to find out how many songs with a popularity score of 0 are there.
print(f'There are {len(dataV2[dataV2['popularity'] == 0])} songs that have a popularity score of 0.')

There are 16019 songs that have a popularity score of 0.

There is a lot of 0 popularity songs, so we decided to pivot our question to 'What song is not as popular as it should be?' Thus, we decided to split our data into 0 popularity songs and non-zero popularity songs.

# Splitting data into a songs with a popularity score above 0 and songs with a popularity score of 0.
dataV3 = dataV2[dataV2['popularity'] != 0]
dataV4 = dataV2[dataV2['popularity'] == 0]

We compared popularity to danceability, we found out that there are too many data points, so we decided to subset the data. This is because we only care about songs that are really popular.

# The graph of popularity vs danceability
corrpd = dataV3['danceability'].corr(dataV3['popularity'])
plt.scatter(dataV3['danceability'], dataV3['popularity'])
plt.xlabel('Danceability', fontsize = 16)
plt.ylabel('Popularity ', fontsize = 16)
plt.title(f'Popularity vs Danceability r = {corrpd.round(2)}', fontsize = 18)

Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Popularity vs Danceability r = 0.06')

We decided to go for the top 5% because the size of the new dataset made it more manageable.

# Subsetting the data into the top 5% of popular
top5popularity = dataV3[dataV3['popularity'] >= dataV3['popularity'].quantile(0.95)]
print(f'There are {top5popularity.shape[0]} songs in the top 5% of the popular songs.')

There are 5472 songs in the top 5% of the popular songs.

From the top 5% we found that popularity and danceability have a weak, positive, linear, fanning outward, correlation. So danceability was not an important trait we should care about, but a danceabilty > 0.5 seems to garner more popular songs.

# Graph of popularity vs danceabilty of the top 5% of popular songs.

Text(0.5, 1.0, 'Popularity vs Danceability of the Top 5% of Popular Songs r = 0.15')

Finding the most popular genres.

# Code that shows how many genres there are.
print(f'There are {len(data['track_genre'].unique())} genres.')

There are 114 genres.

We graphed the difference of the mean and median of the popularity of each genre, because we need to see if we should use the mean or the median to determine the most popular genres. If the difference between the mean and the median of most genres is large enough, then the median would be better, otherwisewe will use the mean. We see that genereally, the difference the mean and the median of the data is not near 0, so we should take the genres with the highest median.

# Graphing og the difference between mean and median
data_AvePop = data.groupby('track_genre')['popularity'].mean()

data_MedPop = data.groupby('track_genre')['popularity'].median()

data_CenterDiff = data_AvePop - data_MedPop
data_CenterDiff = data_CenterDiff.abs().sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
data_CenterDiff.plot(kind='bar', color ='orange')
ax.set_xlabel('Track Genres from Least Difference to Greatest Difference', fontsize = 16)
ax.set_ylabel('Absolute Difference of Mean and Median Popularity', fontsize = 12)
ax.set_title('Histogram of Track Genres', fontsize = 16)
ax.set_xticks([])
plt.show()

# Now we have the top genres
top_genres = data_MedPop.sort_values(ascending=False)
print(f'The top 5 genres are {top_genres.index[0]}, {top_genres.index[1]}, {top_genres.index[2]}, {top_genres.index[3]}, {top_genres.index[4]}.')

The top 5 genres are pop, k-pop, pop-film, hip-hop, chill.

# So we encoded whether the song was a popular genre or not (1 for true, 0 for false)

dum = data_MedPop.sort_values(ascending=False)
dum2 = dum[:5]
pop_genres = dum2.index.to_list()

dataV4['is_pop_genre'] = (dataV4['track_genre']).isin(pop_genres)

# Code for findinging songs that meet our conditions
dataV5 = dataV4[(dataV4['danceability'] > 0.5) & (dataV4['tempo'] > 50) & (dataV4['tempo'] < 200) & (dataV4['energy'] > 0.3) & (dataV4['instrumentalness'] < 0.0001) & (dataV4['danceability'] > 0.5) & (dataV4['is_pop_genre'] == True) & (dataV4['duration_ms'] < 250000) & (dataV4['duration_ms'] > 150000)]
